newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan said mulling food aid for North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Japan said mulling food aid for North Korea.

text.p: A senior U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) official appealed to Japan on Wednesday to extend food aid to North Korea, where widescale famine appeared imminent without urgent supplies.

WFP director Catherine Bertini said she appealed to Japanese Foreign Ministry and agriculture officials and lawmakers for an immediate contribution to an $87 million United Nations emergency food aid package for North Korea.
"The Japanese officials heard what we had to say and they said they will consider it," Bertini told a news conference.
Her warnings were echoed by Red Cross representatives speaking in the South Korean capital Seoul, who said after a visit to the Stalinist North that the country faced imminent catastrophe.
"Without urgent international aid programmes, a large number of North Koreans will face starvation," said Johan Schaar, chief of the Asia-Pacific region of the Geneva-based Red Cross.
The Red Cross officials were in South Korea to supervise the largest shipment of food by South Korean religious and civic groups consisting of food and vegetable seeds worth $1 million.
Bertini was in Japan after a three-day visit to North Korea and said immediate contributions to the WFP campaign alongside 1.1 million tonnes of grain donations were needed urgently.
"If there are not massive amounts of food arriving in the country, people are going to be dying this summer," she said.

"We believe the government can produce one million tonnes, leaving a shortfall of 1.3 million tonnes. Therefore we are appealing to governments to contribute through the WFP and to contribute bilaterally," she said.

Japan, which has no diplomatic relations with North Korea, has held off providing major aid for the northern half of its former Korean colony out of deference to South Korean sensibilities and because of long disputes with Pyongyang.
Bertini said she had seen the early stages of famine -- orange-haired children with distended bellies and people with skeletal arms and legs -- during her visit.
"What we saw gave us a very disquieting sense of inevitability of the tragedy to come... In order to stop the famine we must get people to contribute soon," she said.
"North Korean officials said food supplies will run out in April. We have predicted that they will last until June. The first food shipments will arrive in May," she added.

The 200,000 tonne WFP emergency grain distribution programme had been widened to all children under six years of age and all the country's hospitals, as well as workers in flood-stricken agricultural areas, Bertini said.
Severe floods in 1995 and 1996 devastated crop growing areas in North Korea, causing widepsread food shortages, aid agencies say.
Donor fears of aid being diverted to the country's 1.1-million-strong military could be partly assuaged by WFP assistance in monitoring distribution of bilateral aid, Bertini said.

"Many donors are interested in being sure (aid) goes to very specific people in need. The needs of the vast majority of people must be met by bilateral aid that goes through the public distribution system. The WFP can help in monitoring that, but not all of it."
WFP officials still did not know the severity of the food shortage in the north of the country, which government officials said was worst hit, she said.
A senior government official had told her of people in the north eating tree bark out of desperation, she added.

Japanese television reports of North Korean troop movements to the north near the border with China and of a night blackout imposed in Pyongyang have heightened suspicions of a power struggle between ruling factions.
However, Bertini said she could not confirm reports from North Korean civilian officials of a split with military leaders.
"During our visit we did not talk to any military officials nor get a real sense of the military interest," she said.
